Heavy rains on March 18th brought the Rolling Fork River at Boston barely in flood.  Flood stage at Boston is 35 feet.  The river crested at 35.9 feet around noon on March 20th.

Heavy rains fell across central Kentucky on March 18th.  This brought minor flooding to the Rough River at Dundee on the 19th of March.  Flood stage at Dundee is 25 feet.  The river crested at 25.7 feet late in the morning on March 19th.

Heavy rains around Mammoth Cave National Park on March 18th led to subsequent flooding on the Green River at Woodbury. The river crested at 34.3 feet during the late morning hours on March 20th. Flood stage at Woodbury is 33 feet.

Heavy rain across south central Kentucky on March brought minor flooding to the Green River. This river crested at 17.4 feet at Rochester during the mid-morning hours on March 21st. Flood stage is 17 feet.

A National Weather Service storm survey confirmed a strong, long-tracked tornado that first touched down northwest of Adairville near the intersection of Vick Road and State Highway 96, where a barn sustained roof damage and another outbuilding was destroyed.  This tornado had a 14 mile long track, 9 of which was in Logan County. Overall, this tornado stayed on the ground for 29 minutes.  Damage consistent with a high-end EF-2 tornado was surveyed from near State Highway 96 to just west of the Logan Simpson County line. The worst damage occurred to the north-northeast of Adairville, where the twister crossed Highway 663. Several homes suffered extensive damage. Three people were injured while taking shelter in the bathroom of one home.  A fourth injury occurred at a residence along Trimble Road.  The tornado weakened   as it crossed into Simpson County just north of the intersection of Conn and Reames-Dixon Roads.

A strong, long tracked tornado, which first touched down in Logan County, continued in Simpson County.  The complete track of this twister was just over 14 miles, with the last 4.8 miles in Simpson County.  Earlier, EF-2 damage was surveyed in Logan County, but, by the time it crossed into Simpson County near the intersection of Conn and Reames-Dixon roads, it had weakened to an EF-1.  Several outbuildings and trees were damaged in Simpson County before the tornado lifted along Russelville-Gallatin Road. Overall, 5 homes in both Logan and Simpson Counties sustained extensive damage, with two other residences suffering minor damage. Five grain bins were destroyed.
This hail fell from the supercell thunderstorm that earlier produced an EF-2 tornado well to the west of Franklin.

A spotter reported that hail up to 2 inches in diameter covered the ground just to the east of Franklin.  This hail came from a supercell that earlier had produced an EF-2 tornado well west of Franklin.

The Jefferson County Department of Highways reported street flooding at the intersection of Breckinridge Lane and Interstate 264.  Flooding also occurred at Bashford Manor Lane. The Marion County emergency manager reported street flooding on several locations around the county. In Lebanon, up to 2 feet of water flooded several intersections. Water entered several businesses and blocked a few intersections.
The Casey County emergency manager reported that a road 4 miles northeast of Ellisburg was flooded and partially washed away.
State highway 68, located 2 miles northeast of Gravel Switch, was closed for 45 minutes with around one half foot of water over the road.
A spotter reported one inch hail at the intersection of River Road and Zorn.

A later report from the County Highway Department mentioned a total of over 2 dozen trees downed in the same neighborhood at around the same time.
The public reported a large tree down in Jeffersontown, on the east side of Louisville Metro.
Local law enforcement reported several trees down in Carlisle.
The ASOS instrument measured a 69 mph wind gust at the Fort Knox Airport.
One inch hail fell in Clarksville, just across the Ohio River from Louisville.

A localized downburst brought a few trees down in New Castle.  Local law enforcement reported a few trees toppled along Herndon Lane, as well as Orem and LaGrange Roads.  Another tree was reported downed just to the west of New Castle near the intersection of Highway 146 and Sulfur Road.

A circulation embedded within a strong line of storms spawned an EF-1 tornado that touched down to the northwest of Tell City, in Perry County, Indiana.  It moved southeast for just over 5 miles across Tell City, lifting just south of the intersection of State Highway 237 and Scotch Pine Road.  Several large trees were felled along the entire tornado's path, and several homes in Tell City received damage to their roofs. Numerous outbuildings were destroyed.  A carnival site at the intersection of 10th and Watt Streets was damaged.  A few rides were displaced and a semi-trailer was overturned.  Many tree branches were snapped southeast of Tell City before the tornado lifted.
A spotter reported that numerous trees were downed along Highway 62 between Corydon and Leavenworth.
A Ham Radio operator reported several trees down in the small town of Kellerville, located on State Highway 56 around 9 miles northeast of Jasper.
The Dubois County emergency manager reported numerous trees down in Jasper.

The second of three episodes of heavy rains brought localized flash flooding to Clarksville, which is across the river from Louisville, Kentucky.  Payne-Koelher road was briefly closed due to flooding.
A spotter reported water over New Albany Pike, which is in Clarksville, Indiana. This flooding was associated with the third round of heavy thunderstorms of the day.

The Washington County emergency manager reported that numerous roads across the county were briefly closed by flash flooding. One major road closed was State Highway 150 in Hardinsburg.  The convection behind this specific flooding was the third round of heavy storms of the day. A CoCoRahs spotter nearby in Fredricksburg, Indiana reported over 7 inches of rain for the day.
A spotter reported several roads in Marengo flooded by an overflowing Brandywine Creek.

During the late evening hours, a bowing segment embedded within a lengthy line of storms parallel to and south of the Ohio River began to surge southeast.  On the northeast section of this segment, a reflectivity notch became apparent.  A circulation developed and quickly spawned an EF-2 tornado across northern LaRue County. ||The tornado touched down near the Hardin-LaRue county line between Routes 210 and 61 just northeast of Tonieville.  On Castleman Road, just northeast of the Castleman-Carter Brother's Road intersection, a metal shop had its metal sheeting roof removed and thrown downwind around 100 yards.  Its garage door was bent and insulation was scattered about.  Several trees were uprooted near this location. Damage was estimated as EF-1. ||Downstream, on Carter Brother's Road, a large RV was blown on its side within a mostly destroyed shed.  A two story pole tobacco barn was destroyed.  Many Red and White Oak trees were either sheared off or had lost many large limbs.  Across the road a metal livestock building was destroyed with chaotic damage around a house. Winds here were estimated at around 115 mph, or EF-2.|       |Along State Road 1607, not far from the intersection of Salem Church and Dan Dunn Roads, a silo was caved in and a portion of a corn field flattened.  ||Considerable damage was surveyed along portions of Slack Road.  A one-room schoolhouse was destroyed.  A dairy farm had several buildings destroyed, along with many trees uprooted.  Based on damage to this dairy farm, tornadic winds up to 130 mph were estimated, near the high end of the EF-2 scale.  Also along Slack Road, a two-story house has its entire roof removed.  Blown-in insulation was caked on the entire side of a house.  A shed was destroyed along with a few trees.  The tornado lifted around one fifth of a mile northeast of Nuff Cemetery, near the intersection of Trumbull and Roanoke Roads.

A downpour that quickly brought between one and two inches of rain flooded many low-lying areas and intersections in Louisville. Local broadcast media reported flooded intersections at 3rd Street and Eastern Parkway, Frankfort Avenue at Stocker, and 7th Street's intersection with Oak Street. Water was also reported over Blankenbaker Road near the Southeast Christian Church.
Local media reported that the bottom of the Interstate 65 ramp at Jackson Street was closed due to high water.
The public reported that Frankfort Avenue north of Story Ave. was flooded.
The public reported several flooded roads in Audubon Park.
The local media reported that the intersection of 15th Street and Oak Street was briefly closed due to flooding.
A spotter reported around one half foot of water flowing down Madison Hills and 3rd Street in Richmond.

Local Television media reported a water rescue at Elm Tree Road and East 2nd Street. For the entire day, the Lexington Airport measured 2.75 inches of rain. Most of this fell during the mid-evening hours.
The public reported water over Doylesville Road near Clear Creek. This quickly flowing water was around one half foot deep.
The Franklin County emergency manager reported several trees down in Frankfort.
The local emergency manager estimated that winds up to 70 mph downed several trees in Lewisport.
A spotter reported power lines and trees down on Kentucky 144 just outside of Stephensport.
A HAM radio operator relayed a report of two electric poles snapped on Hillside Drive just outside of Cloverport.
A HAM radio operator reported trees and power lines down along Kentucky Highway 261 just south of McQuady.
The public reported several trees down in Radcliffe, which is near Fort Knox.
A spotter at Freeman Lake Park reported several trees downed and a shed toppled. This park is just north of Elizabethtown.
A spotter reported numerous trees down just south of McDaniels.
Power lines were downed just to the east of Cecilia.
A spotter reported several trees and power lines down in Greensburg.
The public reported several trees down in Campbellsville.
A county official reported tree branches across a power line at mile marker 48 on the Cumberland Parkway.
The local emergency manager reported trees and power lines down across Danville.
The Kentucky Mesonet measured a 58 mph wind gust.  This site is located 3 miles south of Liberty.
A spotter reported several trees down in Russell Springs.
Local media reported trees down in the Font Hill Community, which is located near Lake Cumberland 5 miles east of Jamestown.
The local media relayed a report that a roof was removed from a barn in the town of Salem.
Local media reported that several trees were downed on Kentucky Highway 76 near the town of Webbs Crossroads.
The local broadcast media reported several trees down in the town of Center.
The Marion County emergency manager reported that the siding was ripped off one side of a residence located around 10 miles east of Lebanon. Several large limbs were also snapped.
The public reported a tree down on a house in downtown Liberty.
Heavy rain estimated by radar at over 4 inches in 2 hours brought flash flooding to the intersection of Indiana State Highway 62 and New Buffalo Road.
The Green County emergency manager reported that the intersection of Kentucky Highway 68 and C. Garrison Road was closed due to high water.
The intersection of State Highway South 61 and State Highway 565 was closed due to flash flooding.
A spotter reported quarter sized hail at Mile Marker 7 on Interstate 65.
The Green County emergency manager relayed a report that a measured 3.85 inches of rain fell in a two hour period near the small town of Exie.
A spotter reported several downed trees and limbs in excess of 6 inches in diameter.

A spotter reported 6 TO 7 inches of water flowing over Louisville Road, with water continuing to rise. The ASOS site nearby at the Bowling Green Airport measured over one and one half inches in the 1 1/2 hours previous to this report.
A spotter reported flash flooding at the intersection of Russelville and Morgantown Roads.
A spotter reported flash flooding on Veterans Memorial Lane. The Bowling Green ASOS site nearby at the airport measured 2.77 inches in the 6 hours leading up to this report.
The emergency manager relayed a report of several trees down along Speck Ridge Road.
Multiple trees were downed around Bryantsville.
The Boyle County emergency manager reported many trees down along Lancaster Road, centered around 5 miles east of Danville.
The Kentucky Mesonet measured 1.74 inches of rain in around 50 minutes. This contributed to a small rockslide that briefly closed State Highway 524 just southeast of Westport.

Heavy slow-moving thunderstorms developed north of Madison, Indiana during the late evening. These storms were separate from those that earlier brought flooding to locations southwest of Madison. An estimated 2 to 3 inches fell during a 3 hour window during the mid to late evening hours. Law enforcement reported a car stalled on flooded State Highway 421 just south of the Jefferson-Ripley County Line.
The Jessamine County emergency manager reported several trees down just southeast of Wilmore. This same thunderstorm also brought damage to Garrard and Boyle Counties.

The Taylor County emergency manager reported water over the road at Broadway and Lebanon Avenue in Campbellsville. Many county roads became impassable due to flash flooding, including Meadow Creek Road at Elmore Road and the intersection of Elmore and Davis Roads.
A county official reported that several roads had water flowing over them in Russellville and other portions of northern Logan County.
The Metcalfe emergency manager reported water over State highway 90, making the road impassable.
Holland Road east of Scottsville was impassable due to high water.
A Green County official reported several inches of water on Colombia Highway southeast of Gresham.
The emergency manager relayed a report of 2.35 inches of rain haven fallen in a two hour period.
The Kentucky Mesonet site near Russellville measured over 3 inches of rain in a 3 hour period.

The Logan County emergency manager reported that several people had to be rescued from their homes by boat due to flash flooding. Nearby, 5.3 inches of rain was measured over a 4 hour period ending at midnight CDT.
The local media reported that two boys were rescued after creek waters rose quickly on the Little Indiana Branch in the town of Sadieville.
A vehicle stalled while the driver attempted to drive through up to 4 feet of water covering the road.
A nearby creek overflowed its banks, flooding and briefly closing Robinson Lane, which is just west of Georgetown.
The Frankfort media reported two different water rescues of drivers from their respective vehicles.  One car was stalled in about 12 to 18 inches of water across Country Lane.
Heavy rains flooded and briefly closed the intersection of Country Lane and Saratoga Drive in Frankfort.
An elderly couple were evacuated from their home due to rapidly rising water. Several roads were briefly closed in the Millville area.
Several roads were closed due to high water across Washington County, including State Highway 1039 4 miles southwest of Johnsonville.
Palestine Road became impassable due to high water over the roadway.
The Lexington media reported flooding on Hammonds Creek Road.
Stoner Creek Road near Acton was briefly impassable due to high water.
A car became stalled in high water at a low water crossing on Alton Station Road.  Several Coop and CoCoRah sites measured over 3 inches over an 8 hour period prior to this flooding report.
The Lexington media reported water covering portions of U.S. Highway 68 just southwest of Harrodsburg.
A spotter reported 1.75 inch hail on Goose Creek Road.
The media reported 1.25 inch hail at a rural location 6 miles south southeast of Bardstown.
The Marian County emergency manager reported that a tree was toppled next to State Highway 49.
The public sent several pictures through Facebook of trees split, branches down, and crops flattened near the town of English.
A spotter just south of New Pekin reported that three trees were uprooted.
The local broadcast media reported a large tree down near the small town of Bordon.
Harrison County law enforcement reported trees down county wide, including the town of Corydon.
The public reported numerous trees down with power outages in Floyd's Knobs.
Local law enforcement relayed a report of a house in Fountain Run damaged by lightning.

Local media reported that several trees were downed in the Bashford Manor area and near the Louisville neighborhood of Newburg.  Roof damage was reported as well. This damage was a result of a very localized downburst just south of downtown Louisville that occurred minutes prior to the arrival of a more destructive line of storms.
The public reported power outages and one tree downed on Dixie Highway.
A spotter reported several trees down along State Highway 86 around 7 miles east of Hardinsburg.
The Taylor County emergency manager reported minor street flooding in Campbellsville on Broadway.
ASOS measured a wind gust of 64 mph at Standiford field in Louisville.
A Kentucky Mesonet site, located 10 miles west of Shelbyville, measured a 59 mph wind gust.
The Taylor County emergency manager reported a broken power pole and power lines down on Robinson Avenue in Campbellsville.
Local law enforcement reported trees down in Gamaliel.
Local law enforcement reported a tree down along the 6000 block of Old Boston Road, which is around 2 miles west of Old Boston Road.
Law enforcement reported a tree downed along Buckhorn Drive.
A tree was downed near the intersection of Kidville Lane and Jacks Creek Pike.
The Marion County emergency manager reported a tree down across McCauley Road, which is located around 8 miles west of Lebanon.
Many large limbs were downed along Highway 208 just south of Lebanon.
Local law enforcement relayed a report of one 8 inch and one 15 inch diameter tree branch downed about 5 miles north of Elizabethtown along Sheperdsville Road.
A spotter in Brandenburg reported several large limbs downed.
A spotter reported trees down at Preston Highway and Durrett Lane.
Thunderstorm winds in excess of 60 mph caused a large tree branch to fall on and kill a child at the intersection of Deerfield Avenue and Rudy lane.
The Bullitt County law enforcement reported a tree down across a power line near Pitts Point.
A spotter reported trees down in Brandenburg.
Many trees and several structures were damaged by thunderstorm winds in Campbellsville.
Local law enforcement reported 3 trees downed in Hillview.
One inch hail fell in Lawrenceburg.
Thunderstorms generated a broad gust front that knocked a few trees down in Harrodsburg.
Law enforcement reported damage to a gas station's canopy near the intersection of State Highways 34 and 27.
The Kentucky Mesonet, located 3 miles north of Harrodsburg, measured a 64 mph wind gust at 1150 EDT.
A Kentucky Mesonet site, located 3 miles north of Harrodsburg, measured a 69 mph wind gust at 1155 pm EDT, a full 5 minutes after it earlier measured a 64 mph wind gust.
A creek overflowed its banks in Harrodsburg and covered State Highway 127 with two feet of running water. A car became stalled near this overpass.
Richmond law enforcement reported water over a portion of Interstate 75 associated with a flooded field nearby.
Local law enforcement reported that standing water flooded several cars near Berea.

Heavy rains of up to 5 inches brought flooding to the intersection of Puncheon Creek Road and State Highway 53. Nearby, a house and a church were flooded. An overpass on State Highway 53 was damaged by flooding.
Local law enforcement reported that flooding closed Willisburg Road for around an hour starting shortly after midnight local time.

Shelby County Road Department reported that quite a bit of vegetative debris was left on several roads in the morning from flash flooding that developed shortly after midnight.  Two of these were Cap Ridge and Little Crooked Creek, both located around 4 miles north of Mount Eden.
The 4500 block of Rockbridge Road had to be closed due to flash flooding.

Heavy rains on June 26th brought minor flooding to the Blue River at Fredricksburg during the early morning hours on the 27th.  The river crested at 20.96 feet at around dawn, just over the established flood level of 20 feet.

Emergency dispatch reported temporary road closures and other flooding problems in the Merewood Subdivision in Versailles. Georgia Street and Tyrone Pike were flooded. Some homes on Georgia Street were threatened by rising water.
The public sent an image showing water approaching at least one home on High View Drive.
A Coop observer reported several trees down. A county dispatcher confirmed that power lines were down and several homes were stuck by lightning.
Local media reported golf-ball sized hail that fell from a supercell in Simpsonville.
Hail up to 1.5 inches in diameter was reported along Clark Station Road between Fisherville and Eastwood.
The local emergency manager reported that a large tree fell on a house in Simpsonville.
Local media reported several trees and power lines down near Berea.
A thunderstorm toppled a tree in Richmond.
Local law enforcement reported two trees down along Peaks Mill Road.
The Lancaster Fire Dept. reported that Crab Orchard Road was briefly closed due to flash flooding. Buckeye Road was also partially impeded by high water.
Five hundred feet of Highway 1150 was washed away by flash flooding between mile markers 0 and 1.
Gilbert's Creek Road was closed when Turkey Creek overflowed a bridge.

A Kentucky mesonet site 4 miles north of Stanford measured 2.82 inches of rain in one hour and 10 minutes. This site lies just south of the axis of the heaviest rainfall, where a radar estimated 4 to 5 inches fell with 2 hours.
Lightning struck a tobacco barn near Buckeye, killing two men and injuring 3 others. The men were hanging tobacco at the time.
Minor flooding developed on Stoner Creek during the late evening on July 5th. Flood stage at Paris is 18 feet. Stoner Creek peaked at 19.6 feet at 10 pm on July 5th.
Heavy rains from July 4th through the 6th led to moderate flooding on the Rolling Fork River at Boston. The river crested at 42.2 feet during the late afternoon on July 8th. Flood state is 35 feet.
Heavy rains from the 4th through the 6th of July led to minor flooding on the Green River at Munfordville. Flood stage is 28 feet. The river crested at 31.8 feet during the early evening of July 7th.
The Green river flooded in several locations from the 7th to the 10th of July.  In Brownsville, flood state is 18 feet. The river crested in Brownsville at 21 feet around noon on July 8th.
Heavy rains from the 4th through the 6th of July brought the Green River into flood at Woodbury. Flood state is 33 feet. The river crested at 35.8 feet during the late afternoon on July 7th.

Heavy rains in early July led to flooding on the Green River at several locations. The river flooded Rochester, cresting at 18.2 feet during the early morning hours on the 9th of July. Flood stage at Rochester is 17 feet.
Quarter sized hail was reported by a spotter who lived next to the Warren County Airport.
The Fayette County emergency manager reported several roads closed due to high water across Lexington. Some of these roads include Tahoe, Tate's Creek,and Parker's Mill Roads.
The Lexington Fire Department reported a car swamped in shallow water at the intersection of Leestown and Dolan Roads.
The Lexington media reported several trees down along Old Oxford Road near Georgetown, which is located in Scott County.
The local emergency manager reported trees down in several locations just to the southeast of Lexington.
Local media reported that the roof was partially removed from a trailer on Lisle Road near the Fayette-Scott County line.
Local Lexington media reported trees down along Leestown, Richmond, and Spindletop Roads.

A second round of afternoon thunderstorms brought additional heavy rain to Lexington. Local law enforcement reported that two intersections were closed due to high water. These intersections included River Park and Buelah Roads, and also Leestown and Dolan Roads. Several reports of high water were noted on other portions of Fayette County.
A Garrard County official reported some minor flooding issues across the county, although no roads were closed.

The LaRue emergency manager reported a 29 year old woman was swept away and drowned after driving an ATV into a swollen Otter Creek. This creek empties into the Rolling Fork River, and the accident occurred near this intersection.  Although no rain gauges were located nearby, an estimated 2.5 inches of rain fell within a couple of hours at this site, with more than 3.5 upstream in Marion County.

Local media reports of multiple trees and power lines downed were confirmed by a damage survey along State Highway 146 between Buckner and La Grange.  The survey found two enhanced damage paths brought about by wet microbursts.  The first damage swath was noted along a two mile path along State Highway 146 south of Buckner.  Estimated winds of 70 to 75 mph knocked down numerous trees, large limbs, power poles, electrical lines, and caused some roof damage to barns and homes.  Several telephone poles were snapped along the railroad parallel to KY 146.||The second area of damage developed just downstream of the first area. Several trees were knocked over along State Highway 146 between Kings Lane and Button's Lane. Winds were estimated as between 60 and 65 mph.
Local law enforcement reported three trees down just south of Shelbyville.
Law enforcement from Lancaster reported a few trees down around the town.
Several trees were downed just to the east of Georgetown.
The Fayette County emergency manager reported several trees down around Lexington.
Local law enforcement reported several trees down across Russell Springs.
Jamestown law enforcement relayed several reports of trees down across the city.

The Jefferson County emergency manager relayed a report of damage to some shingles and siding of a home northwest of Madison. a few metallic objects were thrown hundreds of feet. Trees were toppled near the intersection of Chicken Run and Borcherding Roads.

Broadcast media reported 5 injuries from a lightning strike that ended the afternoon racing card at the Kentucky Downs racetrack. Lightning hit a tin pole and traveled down to the ground, shocking 5 people sheltering within a tent. One was transported to a hospital.  The racing board was shorted out with racing cancelled for the rest of the afternoon.
Several trees were downed by thunderstorm winds, damaging a couple of vehicles.
Local media reported that several trees were downed in the Bent Creek subdivision.
Several lanes were blocked by around 1 foot of flowing water near the intersection of Shelbyville Road and Blankenbaker Parkway.
A spotter reported water over KY 1020 just south of Fairdale near Southside Drive. Traffic was halted for a while.

Numerous reports of flash flooding developed across metropolitan Louisville. Several people were rescued from their vehicles in Okolona, Douglass Hills, Edgewood, and Jeffersontown. Flowing water reached the tire tops of several automobiless along Ormsby Lane.
Local media reported that several feet of water accumulated in several basements at the Guardian Court Apartments in Okolona.
Local media reported that several feet of water accumulated on several driveways near the Village Park Apartments.
Several roads were flooded around Medford Lane and Livermore Place.
A spotter reported flooding within the Brookside Apartment Complex and the Hyundai card dealership along Shelbyville Road at Copper Creek Drive.
The  Lexington Emergency Dispatch reported large tree limbs downed near the intersection of Alumni Drive and Turkey Foot Road.
A spotter reported a large tree downed across a road near the intersection of Alexandria and Cambridge Drives. One lane became impassable for a time.
A tree fell across power lines along Standish Way.
Local emergency management reported trees and power lines downed across Paris. Several power outages ensued.
Local media reported several trees downed near Jeffersontown High School. These trees were toppled by a strong convective line of showers.
Gusty winds from a line of strong showers knocked down a tree across a road just to the west of Cloversport. State police had to remove the debris.
A tree fell across the Royal Parkway near Frankfort. A nearby weather station recorded a gust of 58 mph.
The public submitted a picture via Facebook of a large portion of a tree snapped off.
The Bullitt County emergency manager reported that several trees and power lines were downed along Beech Grove Road near Shepherdsville.
Local Lexington media reported several trees downed by a line of convective showers across the city.
The Jessamine County emergency manager relayed several reports of trees and power lines down across the county.
A Kentucky Mesonet site located 10 miles west of Shelbyville recorded a 57 mph wind gust during the passage of a line of showers.
The local media reported that a tree fell through the roof of a home in northern Lexington.

A spotter reported that winds associated with a strong line of showers brought damage to his storm doors and his garage. In his neighborhood many large tree limbs were downed, causing power outages. Thirteen minutes earlier, just 3 miles northwest of Winchester, a Kentucky mesonet site recorded a wind gust of 57 mph.
Quite a few trees and power lines were downed across Lincoln County. In Waynesburg, a tree fell through the roof of a mobile home.

The Waco fire department reported trees down on Goggins Lane and Redhouse Road. Downed trees also blocked Tates Creek Road, Four Mile Road and Summit Street. Nearby, a Kentucky mesonet site measured a 48 mph wind gust. In Richmond, a weather station located at Hummel Planetarium measured a 56 mph wind gust.
Tree branches fell across a power line along Gabbardtown Road, starting a small brush fire. Local wind sensors measured wind gusts up to 45 mph.

A county official reported branches and power lines down across Bowling Green as a result of strong gradient winds. A traffic light at the intersection of Scottsville Road and Interstate 65 was damaged. Local wind sensors measured winds up to 40 mph at this time.

Strong gradient winds felled a large limb of a pecan tree near Hays, KY, killing an elderly woman who was harvesting pecans at the time. A nearby Kentucky Mesonet site clocked winds gusting to 40 mph at the time.
An 18 year old man was injured when his vehicle hit a downed tree on Lyons Station Road. The nearby LaRue County mesonet recorded a 31 mph wind gust at around this same time.
Local media reported damage to a home's deck on Richmond Avenue. The Kentucky mesonet sensor south of Lexington measured a 39 mph wind gust at this time.

A Louisville television station reported several instances of limbs across power lines. Two locations specifically mentioned were located on Martha and East Barbee Avenues.  Winds were gusting above 45 mph at this time.

An EF-1 tornado with maximum winds of 105 mph first touched down just west of Huntsville, located in Butler County.  Damage was first surveyed on Blaine Road where several trees were uprooted.  While moving across Huntsville along Huntsville-Quality road, it damaged a few homes and uprooted additional trees.  Along Silver City-Huntsville road, additional homes and outbuildings were damaged.  A man was injured within a double wide mobile home when its roof and a wall were lifted from the structure.  This injury occurred just west of the intersection of Panther Creek and Silver City-Huntsville Road.  Finally, farther east along Muddy Creek Road, the tornado damaged several additional homes and trees before lifting 4 mile east of Huntsville.
The Orange County police reported that several trees needed to be removed from roadways just northeast of French Lick.
Local law enforcement reported that one telephone pole and a few trees were downed between Delaney Park and Little York.
The Harrison County Road Department had to remove a few trees from a roadway south of the Interstate 64 corridor. One additional tree fell near Elizabeth.

The Clark County, Indiana emergency manager reported that a car drove into standing water near Lakeside Drive. The occupants had to be rescued. This area received between 3 and 4 inches of rain over the previous 6 hours before this rescue.
Nine inches of snow - the highest storm total across southern Indiana - fell near Portersville in Dubois County.
Local media reported a total of 6 inches of snow in Madison, which lies along the Ohio River.
Snow accumulations ranged from near 6 inches in Memphis to around 4 inches across the southern part of the county, directly across the Ohio River from Louisville.
A spotter reported 4 inches of snow in Leavenworth.
A spotter measured 7.5 inches of snow near Hardinsburg.
Louisville media reported 3.5 inches of snow near New Albany. Snow totals were higher across the northwestern portion of the county.
Four and one half inches of snow was measured in Tell City, which lies along the Ohio River.
The media reported 5 inches of snow in Scottsburg.
Several snow measurements ranging between 3 and 4 inches were reported across northern Harrison County.
Spotters reported snowfall amounts varying from 4 to 6 inches of snow across Washington County.

Rain changed to freezing rain around dawn. Two tenths of an inch of glaze developed before precipitation changed over to sleet and snow. Four inches of snow fell across northern Louisville, with just under 3 inches measured along the southern border of the county.

Four inches of snow fell in Milton. Six inches of snow fell along the Ohio River on the northern border of Trimble County. Freezing rain and sleet produced a thin glaze prior to changing over to snow.
Freezing rain deposited around 2 tenths of an inch of ice before changing over to sleet and snow. By late afternoon 3.2 inches of sleet and snow were measured near Buckner.
Several inches of ice, sleet and snow were reported across Henry County. Two tenths of an inch of ice were followed by 2 to 3 inches of sleet and snow.

Freezing rain brought two tenths of an inch of glaze to northern Bullitt County before changing over to sleet and snow. Two to 3 inches of snow fell later in the afternoon across northern Bullitt County.

Freezing rain produced two tenths of an inch of glaze near Fort Knox.  Freezing rain later changed to sleet and snow, with another one to two inches of accumulation along the Ohio River in the northern portion of the county.
Freezing rain produced two tenths of an inch of glaze before changing over to sleet and snow. Three to 4 inches of snow then accumulated through late afternoon along the Ohio River.
Freezing rain deposited up to one quarter of an inch of glaze around the county. Light sleet and snow developed by early afternoon with an inch of additional accumulation.
A quarter of an inch of glaze was deposited by freezing rain during the morning hours. Sleet and snow followed through the late afternoon hours. Five inches of snow was reported near Lewisport.
A spotter in Fordsville reported freezing rain with ice accretions of three tenths of an inch.
A spotter reported that freezing rain deposited one third of an inch of ice by late morning across western Grayson County.
Freezing rain deposited 2 tenths of an inch of glaze on elevated surfaces near Scottsville. This ice toppled a weakened tree onto a home, damaging its roof.

A storm survey confirmed a tornado that damaged the northern portion of Campbellsville. It touched down just west of the intersection of US 68 and Ky 323, where it destroyed several outbuildings. After crossing KY 210, it uprooted trees and damaged several buildings near the intersection of Hodgenville Road and Vintage Lane.  Damage rated as EF-1 was surveyed as the tornado crossed Saloma Road and moved roughly parallel to and just north of Upper Miller Park Road.  Several trees were toppled and several rooftops were damaged.  After crossing the intersection of Eastern Drive and East Lake Drive, it brought additional roof and tree damage to locations near the intersection of US 68 and Palestine Road. At this point, the tornado lifted.

A storm survey confirmed that an EF-1 tornado damaged numerous barns, garages and outbuildings along Dutch Chapel Road. Two homes along this road had significant roof damage. This area of concentrated damage was embedded in a much wider area of lighter damage caused by straight line winds across northern Harrison County. Residents along Dutch Chapel Road reported popping ears and a roaring noise embedded within driving rain and gusty winds associated with a squall line.

A survey confirmed that an EF-1 tornado was embedded within a severe squall line that brought widespread damage to northern Bourbon County.  An area of concentrated damage was surveyed along Colville and Steele Ford Roads as well as Endicott Lane. Along these roads several large barns and outbuildings were either destroyed or heavily damaged. EF-1 damage was confirmed along Endicott Lane as some well-anchored barn footers were lifted up and thrown 75 yards.  Several residents also reported a loud roar within torrential rain as the line of storms passed.

A storm survey confirmed widespread wind damage associated with a squall line around Cave City.  Several businesses had signs blown down or damaged.  A 60 foot tall Super 8 sign next to Interstate 65 was toppled. Trees and power lines were downed.  A grocery store had structural damage, while several other businesses received roof damage.  Wind damage was noted north of Cave City along US 31, where Alvey's Towing Recovery was damaged.  Surveyors estimated straight line winds of between 65 and 70 mph.

A storm survey confirmed widespread damage across southern Hart County east of Horse Cave consistent with straight line winds of 70 to 80 mph. A squall line moved across the area, flipping and destroying a single-wide mobile home just east of Horse Cave. Several barns were destroyed along Highway 218. Many trees were downed as well. On Bunnell Crossing Road near Pascal, a dairy silo was toppled and a barn was extensively damaged. Metal sheeting was removed from this barn and blown downwind for 400 yards.

A storm survey confirmed that sporadic damage across Green County was due to straight line winds up to 65 mph associated with a severe squall line. The most significant damage surveyed was noted in Greenville near the intersection of State Highways 61 and 68, where roof and shingle damage occurred.
A spotter reported several trees down across the western portion of Crawford County.
A spotter reported that a large pine tree was blown down.
A spotter reported a downed tree along Paoli Pike just south of Buffalo Trail.
The local emergency manager reported a few county roads under water. One car became stalled in high water on Greener Road.
Water from Windy Creek covered the road at 16th and Pestalozzi Streets. Several other roads were also flooded.
The Kentucky mesonet in Simpson County measured a 62.5 mph wind gust.
The ASOS at the Bowling Green Airport measured a 62 mph wind gust.  A couple of minutes later, a Kentucky Mesonet site 4 miles east of the airport recorded a 60 mph gust.
The Kentucky Mesonet in Hardin County measured a 67 mph wind gust.
A wind gust of 61 mph was measured in Elizabethtown.
A 67 mph wind gust was measured in Western Edmonson County.
The ASOS site at the Frankfort airport measured a wind gust of 59 mph.
The Kentucky Mesonet in Metcalfe County measured a 70 mph wind gust.
A wind gust of 63 mph was measured by a Kentucky Mesonet site in Anderson County.
A spotter located around 5 miles southwest of Versailles measured a 61 mph wind gust.
The ASOS at the Lexington Airport measured a 66 mph wind gust.
The local media relayed a report of a 72 mph wind gust in Bardstown.
A spotter in Bowling Green on Scottsville Road reported a peak gust of 59 mph. He also reported many trees and power lines down.
The Kentucky Mesonet in Nicholas County measured a 67 mph wind gust.
The Kentucky Mesonet in Franklin County reported a 63 mph wind gust.
High Water briefly closed Connector Road in Bedford.
A spotter reported via HAM radio that KY HWY 60 was under water near the Dollar Store in Irvington.
Heavy rain brought some road closures across the Louisville Metro area, including Preston Highway.
Flashing Flooding was reported on the 500 block of Mill Street in Leitchfield. Around 8 inches of water was running across the road.
Flowing water covered Gaither Station Road, making it impassable.
A HAM Radio operator reported that KY Highway 86 near Lodiburg was closed due to high water.
Metrosafe reported several instances of wind damage across Louisville. One example included a downed tree on Cecil Avenue.

Local law enforcement reported a tree down near Cannon's Lane and Pee Wee Reese Road. Nearby on Cannon's Lane, a spotter estimated a 55 mph wind gust. The ASOS site at nearby Bowman Executive Airport measured a 54 mph wind gust.
Trees were downed on Preston Highway near Bennett Lane.
A HAM Radio operator reported several trees down in Hardinsburg.
Trees were downed in McDaniels.
A spotter reported damage to several signs and porches in Adairville.
A HAM Radio operator reported damage to the roof of a shed.
A HAM Radio operator reported trees down in Vine Grove.

The Simpson County emergency manager reported several trees down in Franklin, including one that blocked Gold City Road. A storm front window was broken on Main Street. Power outages were reported as well.
Several trees were downed in Ratcliffe. Power outages were also reported.
A spotter located in Smith's Grove reported some minor damage to some outbuildings.
Large tree limbs were downed across Highways 61 and 245 near Sheperdsville. A spotter near this same location measured a 50 mph wind gust.
The Priceville law enforcement reported that thunderstorms winds removed a barn's roof. Numerous trees were downed across the county.
Many reports from law enforcement arrived about trees down and power outages across Bowling Green. Debris was scattered across several streets.
A storm survey found that several hardwood trees were downed along Pleasant Valley Road near the intersection with Coakley Road. Wind speeds were estimated at 65 mph.
The public reported that several trees were downed in Gamaliel and other locations around Monroe County.
The public reported via Twitter of a tree downed across Old Sheep Pen Road west of Frankfort.
The county emergency manager reported that many trees were downed in Woodford County, with a concentration along Old Frankfort Pike and Midway Road.
The Boyle County emergency manager reported several trees and power lines downed across Danville.
A tree was downed on a residential property in the Indian Hills Subdivision.
The county road commission reported that several large trees were downed along with multiple power lines just east of Lawrenceburg along US 62 between Starhill Way and Lock Drive.
The public reported via Twitter that two barns were destroyed near Western Elementary School.  Several signs were twisted as well.
Nicholas County emergency management reported numerous downed trees blocking roads across the county.
Many reports arrived concerning downed trees, power lines and blown transformers south of Wilkinson Road and north of east Main Street in Frankfort.

A reporter from the Hawesville newspaper provided information about a home on Goering Road that was badly damaged by winds estimated at 70 mph. The home lost its front porch and a section of an attached roof. A nearby barn was destroyed. The house's attached garage had its door blown in, with a section of the garage's back wall bowed out.
A trained spotter with a reliable anemometer measured an 82 mph wind gust at his residence. His location fell within an area where numerous other damage reports were received.
A former National Weather Service employee measured around 6.5 inches of snow near Goshen. Several other spotters measured 5 inches, including one in Pee Wee Valley.

The official snow total measured at Standiford field in Louisville was 3.8 inches. Several unofficial reports of 4 to 5 inches arrived from northeastern Jefferson County. An arctic front arrived just after 7am, during the morning rush hour. Icy roads and reduced visibilities due to blowing snow lead to numerous traffic accidents.
Snowfall totals of between 4 and 5 inches were reported across Henry County.
Six inches of snow was measured in Madison, along the Ohio River in Jefferson County, Indiana.
Four inches of snow was measured in Bordon. By 10 am, 5 inches of snow had fallen in Henryville.
Four and one half inches of snow was measured in Austin.
The local fire department located just north of Albany measured 4.5 inches of snow.
Four inches of snow fell overnight in Jeffersonville, which is right across the Ohio from Louisville.
Around 4 inches of snow fell in New Albany, which is right across the River from Louisville.
An observer measured around 3.3 inches of snow near Hawesville. Elsewhere several reports of 4 inches were received.
A spotter reported 4.5 inches of snow in Irvington, which is right on the border of Breckinridge and Meade Counties.
A snow total of 4.5 inches was reported in Irvington, which is adjacent to Meade County.
Four inches of snow fell right along the Ohio River near Fort Knox.
Six inches of snow was measured near Mount Washington, which is in northern Bullitt County.
An observer at Standiford International Airport measured 5 inches of snow. Six inches of snow fell at the National Weather Service office in southern Jefferson County.
Four inches of snow was measured near La Grange.
Over 6 inches of snow was measured near Pleasureville, which is located in southern Henry County.
Snowfall was measured at 6.8 inches in Shelbyville.
A COOP observer measured 5.5 inches in Taylorsville.
A resident just south of Frankfort measured 5.5 inches of snow.
Four inches of snow fell near Georgetown.
Just over 5 inches of snow was measured in Cynthiana.
Around 4 inches of snow fell near Carlisle.
A COOP observer measured 4 inches of snow in Paris.
An observer at the Lexington Airport measured 4 inches of snow. In general, around 3 inches of snow fell across Lexington.
Several locations in northern Woodford County averaged around 4 inches of snow.
Around 3 to just over 4 inches of snow fell across Northern Anderson County.

A mix of sleet, snow and freezing rain severely affected traffic during the overnight period across Ohio County. In Hartford, 2.5 inches of sleet and snow accumulated. During the evening hours, a man was killed when his vehicle was hit by a snowplow during poor visibility. The collision occurred at the intersection of State Highway 231 South and Lee Drive.
Three inches of snow was measured in Bardstown.  Farther north, heavier snow fell, accumulating to around 4 inches.
A mixture of freezing rain, sleet and snow fell across Grayson County, hampering overnight traffic.  Around 2 inches of sleet and snow was measured north of Leitchfield.

Around one quarter of an inch of ice accumulated on elevated surfaces near Hodgenville. Substantial icing, accompanied by one half inch of sleet, made driving treacherous during the early morning hours.
A spotter in Elizabethtown - in southeast Harrison County, west of Louisville - measured 4.5 inches of snow.

Over 2 1/2 inches of rain fell on partially frozen ground across Warren County within a 6 hour period. With such poor drainage, water covered many roads in the Bowling Green area, rendering some impassable. State Highway 622 was closed for a short time near Plano.
The Bowling Green media reported that a portion of State Highway 100 was blocked by flowing water a few miles west of Franklin.
A picture sent on twitter indicated over one third of an inch of ice on a tree branch.
The Madison County emergency manager reported several large tree branches downed with power outages in Richmond and Berea. He estimated ice accumulations of one quarter of an inch.

The ASOS ice sensor at the Lexington Airport measured 0.37 of an inch of ice. This icing developed over a period of time when just over one inch of freezing rain fell. The temperature hovered around 30 or 31 for much of the event. Sporadic tree damage and power outages were reported in Lexington.

Ice accumulations of one quarter to one third of an inch downed numerous trees across Louisville and the rest of Jefferson County. Sporadic power outages developed. One National Weather Service employee had a 50 foot pine tree fall across her fence.
Icing, with accumulations of near one quarter of an inch, downed several trees across the county.
Emergency management reported that ice accumulations up to one quarter of an inch led to numerous downed trees and power lines across the county.
Just over one quarter of an inch of ice was measured near Shepherdsville. Some power lines were downed across the county.
A NWS forecaster measured one quarter of an inch of ice in Vine Grove.
One quarter of an inch of ice was measured in Paris.
One quarter of an inch of ice accumulated on branches near Buffalo.
A National Weather Service Employee measured one quarter of an inch of ice.
Ice accumulations of one third of an inch were reported for various locations in Shelby County. Several trees and power lines were downed.
Icing up to one third of an inch brought scattered reports of downed trees and power lines countywide.
One third of an inch of ice formed on elevated surfaces near Lewisport. A second report from the public mentioned 2 inches of snow and one quarter of an inch of ice accretion near the same location.
One quarter of an inch of ice was measured on an elevated surface near Garfield.
The police department in Milton reported between one half inch and one inch of sleet and snow, followed by one quarter of an inch of ice.
One quarter of an inch of ice was measured on elevated surfaces in Frankfort. The ASOS ice accretion sensor at Frankfort measured 0.31 inches of ice.
Several locations around Georgetown received over one quarter of an inch of ice.
One quarter of an inch of ice downed several trees around the county.
Several locations around Cynthiana received around one quarter of an inch of ice.
Several locations measured ice accretions between one quarter to one third of an inch of ice.
One quarter of an inch of ice was measured on an elevated surface near Bardstown.
Ice accumulations averaged around one third of an inch near Lawrenceburg.
Around one third of an inch of ice accumulated on elevated surfaces near Versailles.
Brief heavy snow developed during the afternoon. This changed over to sleet and freezing rain by late afternoon. Two to three inches of snow was quickly followed by a quarter of an inch of ice.
Brief heavy snow and sleet accumulated to around one half inch before changing to freezing rain by late afternoon. One quarter to one third of an inch of ice downed a few trees and power lines.
An observer measured 5 inches of new snow to the north of French Lick. From 3 to 5 inches of snow fell across the county, followed by a quarter of an inch of ice.
A trained spotter reported 4 to 5 inches of snow across the county. Heavy snow fell for around 3 hours, followed by one quarter of an inch of ice. Several trees were downed due to icing.
Heavy snow accumulated from one to two inches before changing over to sleet and freezing rain. One quarter of an inch of ice accumulated on elevated surfaces.
Heavy snow accumulated to 2 inches near Bristow, before changing briefly to sleet and then freezing rain. Countywide, one quarter of an inch of ice formed on elevated surfaces.
A spotter near Marengo measured just over 2 inches of snow before a changeover to sleet and then freezing Rain. Ice accumulated around one quarter of an inch countywide.

Heavy snow developed during the late afternoon hours. It brought around one to three inches countywide over a 2 hour period before changing briefly to sleet and then freezing rain. Ice accumulations reached a quarter of an inch.
A spotter near Austin measured 2 inches of snow before it changed over to sleet and freezing rain. Ice accumulations exceeded one quarter of an inch countywide.
Snow and sleet accumulated to around one inch before changing over to freezing rain. Ice accumulated around one quarter of an inch on elevated surfaces.
The county emergency manager reported numerous limbs downed with sporadic power outages due to icing. Between one quarter and one third of an inch of ice accumulated on elevated surfaces.
Ice across Grayson County accumulated from one quarter to one third of an inch. A few hundred customers lost power. Many large tree limbs were downed.
Ice accumulated over one quarter of an inch on elevated surfaces countywide. Many limbs were downed, causing sporadic power outages.
Ice accumulated to just over one quarter of an inch on elevated surfaces.
Freezing rain brought ice accumulations of over one quarter of an inch to elevated surfaces.
A large tree was downed due to ice accumulation near Roundhill.  According to this report, just under one third of an inch accumulated on elevated surfaces.
Snow accumulations of around 4 inches were reported near Paoli.
Just under 4 inches of snow fell near New Pekin.
Local media reported that up to 5 inches of snow fell near Milltown, which is in northeastern Crawford County.
Local Louisville news reported 4 inches of snow in Bordon.
The Scott County emergency manager relayed several reports of 4 inches of snow across the county.
Local media reported 4 inches of snow in Madison, which is just across the Ohio River from Trimble County.
Several location across Trimble County received just over 4 inches of snow.
A spotter in Campbellsburg measured 4 inches of snow.
A patrolman relayed a report of 5 inches of snow on the roads near Antioch.
Several trees were downed across the county. One tree was toppled just east of Scottsburg.
Local media relayed a report of an estimated 60 mph wind gust near New Pekin. Several trees were toppled in and around the town.
The Kentucky Mesonet site near Franklin measured a 64 mph wind gust.
The Kentucky Mesonet site near Burkesville measured a 59 mph wind gust.
Scottsville law enforcement reported several trees down just south of Scottsville.
Local Law enforcement reported several trees down in Halfway.
The Ohio County emergency manager reported that several roads were blocked by downed trees in Rosine.
The Adair County emergency manager reported that a tree was downed in Columbia. Numerous power outages were reported around town as well.
The Lexington Police reported several trees down across town.
Local media reported numerous power outages near Jamestown.
The Madison County emergency management reported that debris covered a portion of Dayview Road in Richmond.
Several trees were downed near the intersection of Carver's Ferry and Charles White Roads. This intersection is just to the southwest of Valley View.

Several trees were downed across the county, including one on Sulfur Licks Road north of Frankfort. Another tree was reported down along US 421 north of Frankfort.  A trained spotter east of Frankfort measured a 57 mph wind gust.
Heavy rains across the Bluegrass Region on the 5th and the 6th led to minor river flooding at Paris. Stoner Creek rose to 18.5 feet during the late evening on the 6th. Flood state is 16 feet.

Widespread heavy rains of around 2 inches fell across central Kentucky during the evening hours on Dec 21st. This led to minor flooding on the Rough River at Dundee. The river crested at 25.1 feet just before midnight on the 22nd.  Flood state is 25 feet.

Widespread heavy rains during the afternoon and evening hours on the 21st of December led to minor flooding of the Blue River at Fredricksburg. Flood stage is 20 feet, and the river crested at 12.4 feet around noon on the 22nd.

Heavy rains across the Bluegrass Region on the 5th and the 6th (in advance of the cold air intrusion that occurred on the 6th) led to minor river flooding at Paris. Stoner Creek rose to 18.5 feet during the late evening on the 6th. Flood state is 16 feet.

The Nelson County emergency manager confirmed that 3 out of 5 occupants of an SUV died after it ran into water covering a low water crossing on Dee Head Road, which is located around 2 miles southeast of New Haven. Two people were rescued, but 3 drowned within the SUV.  Heavy rain throughout the day on the 21st caused rapid rises in area creeks and streams. The vehicle was washed away at this crossing at around 3 am local time on the 22nd of December.
In Columbia, the Adair County emergency manager reported light icing, followed by 2 inches of sleet and then 3 inches of snow.
The emergency manager reported around one quarter of an inch of ice, followed by 5 inches of sleet and snow combined.
The Boyle County Highway Department reported up to one quarter of an inch of icing, followed by 2 inches of sleet and then 4 inches of snow.
Just over 5 inches of snow followed a half inch of sleet and a light glaze of ice.
The emergency manager relayed a report of an accumulation of two inches of sleet followed by 3 inches of snow.
Icing of up to two tenths of an inch was followed by 1 inch of sleet and 4 inches of snow.
Sleet accumulated one quarter of an inch before changing to snow.  Four inches of snow was measured in Carlisle.
A third of an inch of sleet fell before changing to all snow, which then accumulated around 4 inches near Newtown.
Around 5 inches of snow fell on top of 1 to 2 inches of ice and sleet.
The Garrard County emergency manager reported that around 3 and one half inches of snow fell on on top of one and one half inches of sleet.
Freezing rain brought a tenth of an inch of ice, before changing into sleet. Over 2 inches of sleet fell before precipitation changed into snow, bringing another 2 to 3 inches.
Over 4 inches of sleet and snow fell in Lawrenceburg.
An observer reported that freezing rain brought up to one quarter of an inch of icing before changing to sleet and then snow. Four inches of sleet and snow were measured near Greensburg.
Freezing rain brought a tenth of an inch of ice before changing over to sleet and freezing rain.  Three inches of sleet and snow were measured at both Upton and Hodgenville.
Heavy sleet accumulated to over 2 inches in Burkesville before changing over to snow. After the changeover, 2 to 3 inches of snow fell.

Freezing rain brought a glaze of around one tenth of an inch before changing to sleet and snow. Near Salem, sleet accumulated to around 1 and one half inches before changing to snow. An additional one to two inches of snow fell after that.

Freezing rain with light icing changed to sleet and snow. At Cumberland City, over 1 inch of sleet fell before changing to snow. Snowfall amounts then varied from near 2 inches near Russell County to less than one inch near the Tennessee Border.

A spotter near Scottsville reported freezing rain with icing amounts between one quarter and one half inch. This brought isolated power outages around the county. Freezing rain changed to sleet and then snow with another one and one half of an inch accumulation.

Ice deposited around one tenth of an inch of ice before changing over to sleet and then snow.  One to 3 inches of sleet and snow then fell with the higher amounts across the northern portion of the county.

Freezing rain brought icing of one tenth of an inch before changing to sleet and snow. Significant sleet brought accumulations from 1 to 2 inches before changing to snow. An additional 2 inches of snow fell.

The Lexington media reported from 4 to 5 inches of snow and sleet. Light freezing rain preceded this with icing of around one tenth of an inch. The snow observer at the Lexington airport measured a storm total of 5 inches of snow and sleet.

Freezing rain brought icing measured at between one and two tenths of an inch. Precipitation then changed to sleet with substantial accumulations of between one and two inches. Snow brought an additional one to two inch accumulation.
Between 4 and 5 inches of snow and sleet fell near Winchester.
Substantial sleet brought accumulations of around 2 inches before changing to snow. Snow brought an additional 2 to 3 inches.

Freezing rain brought a light glaze before changing over to sleet and snow. Sleet then accumulated to around 1 inch before changing over to snow. Total sleet and snow accumulations averaged between 4 and 5 inches across the county.
Light freezing rain changed to sleet, then snow. Sleet and snow accumulations averaged around 4 inches.
Freezing rain during the late afternoon changed over to sleet and then snow by early morning. Four inches of sleet and snow fell near Cynthiana.
Snow and sleet accumulations of 5 inches were reported near Brownsville. Sleet alone accounted for 2 inches of this total.

Light freezing rain brought icing of around one tenth of an inch before changing to sleet. Substantial sleet accumulations of 2 inches were measured before changing over to snow, bringing another 2 inches of accumulation.

Freezing rain during the late afternoon brought a light glaze of ice before changing over to sleet by evening. Substantial sleet accumulations of over 2 inches fell near Bowling Green before changing over to snow. An observer in Bowling Green measured 4. 8 inches of sleet and snow.

Freezing rain brought a glaze of between one and two tenths of an inch of ice. Sleet then developed, accumulating around 1 inch before changing to snow. Snow continued through the morning hours on the 3rd, bringing an additional 3 inches.
Freezing rain brought a light glaze before switching over to sleet and then light snow. Substantial sleet accumulations of between 1 and 2 inches were measured before light snow brought another inch.

Freezing rain brought icing of around one tenth of an inch before switching over to sleet during the late evening. Substantial sleet accumulations of up to 2 inches developed before precipitation changed over to light snow. An additional inch of snow fell.

A spotter in Salem reported that one quarter inch of ice covered surfaces by early afternoon. Later that evening, sleet accumulated up to one half inch before ending as light snow with an additional accumulation of 1 to 2 inches.

A spotter in English reported ice accumulations of one quarter of an inch by early afternoon. Later that evening sleet accumulated up to one half inch before changing to snow. One to two inches of snow fell before ending during the early morning hours on the 3rd.
Freezing rain produced an icy glaze of one quarter of an inch by early afternoon on the 2nd. Later that evening, sleet and snow added another 2 inches.
Freezing rain deposited a quarter of an of ice during the morning hours of March 2nd. Later that evening, a combination of sleet and snow brought another 2 inches.
Freezing rain during the morning hours on the 2nd produced around 2 tenths of an inch of ice. Later that evening, a round of sleet and snow produced just under 4 inches near Tell City.
Freezing rain produced around 2 tenths of an inch of ice.  Later that evening, sleet and snow developed, adding another 2 to 3 inches of accumulations before ending by early morning.
Freezing rain brought ice accumulations of 2 tenths of an inch during the morning hours on the 2nd. Later that evening, additional snow and sleet added another 1 to 2 inches of accumulation.

During the morning hours on the 2nd, freezing rain brought around 2 tenths of an inch of ice. Later that evening, sleet and snow brought an additional 3 inches before ending during the early morning hours.

Freezing rain during the morning of the 2nd brought around 2 tenths of an inch of ice. Later that evening significant sleet accumulated over one half inch. Sleet then changed to snow by the early morning hours on the 3rd. Additional snow accumulations totaled 2 to 3 inches.

Freezing rain brought ice accumulations to around one quarter of an inch during the morning hours on the 2nd. Later that evening, a round of sleet and snow brought an additional accumulation of 1 to 2 inches.

Freezing rain during the evening of the 2nd brought ice accumulations of around one quarter of an inch. This turned into sleet and then snow by late evening.  One half inch of sleet accumulated, followed by 2 to 3 inches of snow.

Light freezing rain changed to sleet and then snow during the late evening on the 2nd. A glaze of one tenth of an inch of ice was followed by one half inch of sleet and another 2 inches of snow before ending the next morning.

Light freezing rain deposited one tenth of an inch of ice before turning into sleet during the evening of the 2nd. Sleet accumulated to around 4 tenths of an inch before turning into light snow. Two inches of snow accumulated before ending the next morning.
An observer reported 4 inches of snow near Bedford.

Light freezing rain deposited a tenth of an inch of ice during the morning hours on the 2nd. After a several hour break in precipitation, sleet and snow developed during the afternoon. Around 4 inches of sleet and snow accumulated north of New Castle.
An observer measured 2 inches of combined sleet and snow near New Haven. Across the southern portions of Nelson County, sleet accumulations varied from one half to one inch.
A NWS employee in Vine Grove measured 3 inches of snow and sleet. Considerable amounts of sleet fell across the southern portion of the county, with accumulations between one half and one inch.
An observer just west of Frankfort measured just under 3 inches of sleet and snow. Of this amount, over one half inch fell as sleet.
An observer near La Grange measured 2.5 inches of snow and sleet at 7 am on the morning of the 3rd. Additional snow after the measurement added another inch to the total.
An observer northwest of Taylorsville measured 4 inches of snow and sleet.
An observer near Shepherdsville measured 2.5 inches of snow and sleet. Of this amount, just less than one half inch was sleet.
Between 3 and 4 inches of snow and sleet were reported from several locations around the county.

Just under 3 inches of snow and sleet fell during evening of March 2nd, ending during the early morning on the 3rd. During the morning hours on the 2nd, freezing rain brought a light glaze throughout the Louisville metropolitan area.

Light freezing rain that began during the late afternoon brought icing up to a quarter of an inch before changing into sleet and then snow. Sleet and snow accumulations reached 2 to 3 inches before ending as snow during the early morning hours.

Freezing rain that began during the late afternoon on the 2nd brought a glaze of around one quarter of an inch before changing to sleet and snow by late evening. Sleet and snow accumulations reached 2 to 3 inches before precipitation ended early on the 3rd.

Freezing rain during the afternoon on the 2nd brought a light glaze of ice before changing over to sleet and then snow by early on the 3rd. Along with the icing, 2 to 3 inches of sleet and snow fell across the county.
A rain gauge near Sellersburg associated with the Louisville Metropolitan Sewer District measured 4.49 inches within a 36 hour period.
The Louisville media relayed a report from the public that 4 1/2 inches of rain had fallen within 24 hours just north of New Albany.
A spotter measured just over 4 inches of rain within a 40 hour period.
Flash flooding briefly closed Indiana State Highway 56 in French Lick.
A CoCoRahs observer reported numerous streets and intersections flooded across Jasper, especially along the Patoka River.
Lick Creek, in Paoli, overflowed it banks and brought flooding to State Road 37.

The local police reported that water covered numerous intersections within Marengo, including State Highway 66. One family was evacuated from their home due to threatened flooding. In English, emergency personnel had to respond to a stalled car at the intersection of State Roads 237 and 64.
Mulberry Street was flooded and became briefly impassable.
Several intersections in New Pekin were briefly impassable due to high water.
Dean Road, located in Sellersburg, was flooded and became briefly impassable.
Excessive rains brought about a mudslide, which closed one lane on Interstate 64, near its intersection with Interstate 265.
Water flooded U. S. Highway 150 where it crossed over Little Indian Creek.
The Floyd County emergency manager reported that several water rescues were performed in New Albany from stalled vehicles in flooded intersections.
The Grayson County emergency dispatch relayed a report concerning golf-ball sized hail that cracked windshields.
A swath of large hail stretching all the way back west towards Caneyville brought 1.75 inch hail to Leitchfield.
The Kentucky Mesonet near La Grange measured over 4 and 1/2 inches of rain over a 36 hour period.
Local law enforcement reported that State Highway 1606, located just west of Campbellsburg within the flood plain of the Little Kentucky River, was flooded in several locations.
Highway 421 flooded just to the north of New Castle.
A spotter reported water over the road on State Highway 69 between Fordsville and Hartford. Traffic was briefly redirected.
High water made several roads along State Highway 70 in eastern Taylor County impassable, including Acton, Bradfordsville, and Palestine Roads.
An employee reported around one foot of water over Hammonsville Road near Laton-Turner road due to an overflowing creek.
State Highway 222 was briefly closed by high water as the Nolin River overflowed its banks.

Widespread heavy rains of 3 to locally over 5 inches led to moderate flooding on the Blue River at Fredricksburg. The river exceeded its flood stage of 20 feet early on the 4th of April. It peaked at 23.77 feet late on the 4th before falling below flood stage early on the 5th.

Widespread 2 to 3 inch rains on April 3rd and 4th led to minor flooding of the Green River at Woodbury a day later.  Flood stage at Woodbury is 33 feet.  The river peaked at 34 feet just after midnight on the 5th of April.
A tree fell on power lines along Nutwood Street near T. C. Cherry School.
The Warren County emergency dispatch reported power-lines down along East 14th Avenue.
A spotter reported snapped trees along Beech Bend Road just outside of Bowling Green.

A report via twitter mentioned that a large tree was downed along Massey Road near Detour Road.  Nearby, at nearly the same time, the roof was removed from an outbuilding near Day Road's intersection with Kentucky State Road 185.
Local law enforcement reported several trees downed near Bardstown. Trees were toppled near South Kennett Avenue, Barton Road, and Edelen Avenue.

Several reports arrived from Shelbyville of damage associated with thunderstorm winds. A report arrived via Facebook of a tree down in downtown Shelbyville, and local media reported damage to a resident's skylight in northern Shelbyville. A home weather station 2 miles southeast of town measured a 50 mph wind gust.
Emergency dispatch reported several trees down across the northern and eastern portions of Shelby County.
Emergency management reported several trees downed on Lead Mine Road near the Owen County border.

Widespread heavy rains on the 3rd and the 4th of April brought minor flooding to the Rough River at Dundee. Flood stage is 25 feet. The river crested at 27.4 feet during the early morning hours on the 5th.
Heavy rains April 3rd and 4th brought minor flooding to the Rolling Fork River at Boston. Flood stage at Boston is 35 feet. The river crested at 36.7 feet just after midnight on the 6th of April.

Minor flooding on Drake's Creek near Alvaton resulted from heavy rains around Bowling Green on the 3rd and 4th of April. Flood stage is 22 feet. Drake's Creek crested at 23.6 feet during the early morning hours on April 4th.

Minor flooding developed on the Green River at Rochester as a result of heavy rains earlier across south central Kentucky. Flood stage at Rochester is 17 feet. The river crested at 17.9 feet during the early morning hours hours.

The Ohio river at the Tell City water treatment plant barely crept over flood stage due to previous heavy rains across southern Indiana and central Kentucky. The Ohio reached 38.6 feet at Tell City during the early morning hours on the 6th. Flood stage is 38 feet.
Louisville local media relayed a report of 1.25 inch hail and winds that gusted to 50 mph. An off duty Weather Service employee located 2 miles away reported one inch hail at the same time.
A spotter reported one inch hail covering Veterans' Parkway.
A spotter reported that flash flooding briefly closed State Highway 403 just west of Woodbury.
A spotter in Leopold measured a 63 mph wind gust. He also noted pea sized hail.
One inch hail fell one mile north of Leavenworth.
Local law enforcement reported 1.5 inch hail 2 miles north of St Croix.
A spotter reported 1 inch hail in Sulfur.
A spotter in Beechwood reported golf ball sized hail.
A spotter reported dime and quarter sized hail.
The Dubois County emergency manager reported that a pole barn with its doors open was blown down.
A new barn, with its doors open to its east, was destroyed when thunderstorm winds entered the structure.
Three and one quarter inches of rain fell in a 2 hour period in Tell City. Flowing water was reported on Franklin Street when Windy Creek exceeded its banks.
Water overflowed U.S. Highway 150 at two places. The highway was briefly closed.
Many roads across Tell City and other locations in Perry County became impassable due to flash flooding.
The County Road Commission reported that Tom Bolin Road near State Highway 271 was closed due to high water.
An off duty NWS employee driving on Interstate 64 just northwest of Lexington reported 1 inch hail covering the Interstate and significantly slowing traffic.
The Lexington media reported 1.25 inch hail just southeast of Versailles.
A section of a roofing cover was blown off of a building.
A few inches of water covered Trojan Trail Road near 31E.
Lexington media reported that lightning downed a large tree near Cross Keys Road, which fell across several power lines. This brought widespread power outages.

An EF-0 tornado with estimated winds between 65 and 80 mph touched down and snapped a tree at a residence along Lotus Street. It then moved northeast and removed several shingles from another home along this same street. Several large branches were downed near this home as well. Several trees were also toppled in a wooded area behind this home.  A neighbor along Deatsville Road had a tree fall and crush a trampoline.  Farther north along Deatsville Road, a resident lost a large section of a tree and had minor siding damage along the east side of his home.  A mile farther to the northeast, just before lifting, the tornado sheared off a portion of a row of trees adjacent to Maraman Road.  The maximum wind speed was estimated based on snapped 1 to 2 foot diameter tree trunks. Structural damage resulted from winds estimated at 65 to 70 mph.
Hanging Rock Hill Road was closed due to high water. A radar estimated rainfall of 2 to 3 inches fell within a two hour period.
A spotter just west of Madison reported 1 inch hail.
Quarter sized hail was reported in Sellersburg.
A spotter 2 miles southwest of Sellersburg saw 1 inch hail.
Local media relayed a report of 1.25 inch hail just north of Interstate 64 in New Albany.
A storm that interacted with a previous boundary briefly acquired supercell characteristics and produced golf ball sized hail near Riddle.
A spotter reported a large amount of quarter sized hail that whitened the ground just northeast of Sulfur Springs.
Local law enforcement reported that a tree fell onto a home in Salem.
The Scott County emergency management reported several trees down countywide.
New Salisbury law enforcement reported a tree down across a road.
The Lexington media reported that lightning struck a church steeple in Georgetown, starting a small roof fire.
The ASOS at the Bluegrass Airport west of Lexington measured a 57 mph wind gust.
The Kentucky Mesonet site 3 miles north of Harrodsburg measured a 65 mph wind gust.
The Kentucky Mesonet several miles south of Frankfort measured a 60 mph wind gust. Several miles north, the Frankfort Airport ASOS measured a 48 mph gust.
A 68 mph wind gust was measured by a Kentucky Mesonet site 2 miles east of Hodgenville.
Local law enforcement reported several trees down centered around Bethlehem.
Scott County emergency management reported trees down along Pea Ridge Road and other locations along the Franklin/Scott County Line.
A spotter reported a tree down near 1004 Lloyd Road.
The local media reported numerous power lines downed by an outflow boundary ahead of a thunderstorm.
A NWS employee reported several trees down in his neighborhood 1 mile west of Pee Wee Valley. Twelve miles farther north, a Kentucky Mesonet site measured a 51 mph wind gust.
Multiple trees were downed within an area extending from Shelbyville west to the Jefferson County line. Several roads were blocked.
In Shelbyville, siding was ripped off of a residence. Around town, several trees and traffic lights were downed.
Local law enforcement reported trees down along Eastwood...Fisherville Road.
A spotter reported large limbs downed by estimated 65 mph wind gusts.
Local law enforcement reported multiple trees down near the intersection of Tate's Creek and East Hickman Roads. Two miles to the west at around the same time, a tree fell on a garage.
Local media reported minor roof damage at an auto parts store.
A bowing segment brought widespread power outages throughout the county.  Several trees were downed in Richmond.
Highway 34 north of Danville was closed for an hour due to the removal of downed trees. In general, a bowing segment downed many trees countywide.
A bow echo downed multiple trees across the county, including some in Lancaster.
The Boyle County emergency manager reported that 3 trees had fallen along Airport Road near Junction City.
Local law enforcement reported trees down throughout the county. At 925 pm EDT, the Kentucky Mesonet 4 miles northeast of Stanford measured a 51 mph wind gust.
A few large trees were toppled near Middleburg.
Ping Pong ball sized hail fell near the town of Bugtussle.

A storm survey confirmed damage from a wet microburst that damaged many trees and several buildings just northwest of Ratcliff. The area surveyed covered an area roughly one half mile wide and 2 to 3 miles in length. Based on damage, northwest winds gusted as high as 70 to 75 mph. Along with many downed trees, two homes on Kingswood Road near Hillcrest Road had large sections of their roof taken off and thrown several hundred yards to the southwest. Several homes on Scenic Drive has substantial garage and siding damage. Two businesses at a strip mall just off of Highway 31W had sections of their roof damaged. Hail up to penny size fell for 20 minutes and produced some drifts up to one foot high.

A storm survey confirmed widespread straight line wind damage in Hodgenville. A compact but fast moving bow echo that earlier damaged Radcliff brought a measured wind gust of 68 mph to a Kentucky Mesonet site just west of Hodgenville.  Numerous soft and hardwood trees had either toppled or had had branches stripped and thrown in a southeasterly direction.
